title: One request, three independent gates - and what each one catches if the others fail

children.title: LAYER C - Identity Proxy (the bouncer)
lines: Terminates TLS · verifies the session/JWT · extracts app + owner from the URL · adds X-App-ID · no raw port is ever exposed
What it does NOT catch: anything that happens AFTER a legitimate, authenticated user is already inside their own workspace.
If this were the only layer: a legitimate user runs malicious code inside their own container - the proxy only watches the front door, never sees this "east-west" traffic.

children.title: LAYER B - VLAN / ipvlan (the soundproof wall)
lines: Every tenant's traffic is 802.1Q-tagged (vlan.id) on a dedicated sub-interface · the kernel makes cross-tenant packets physically unroutable
What it does NOT catch: a kernel escape on the host itself.
If this were the only layer: a zero-day in the real Linux kernel lets an attacker break out of runc entirely - from there, one `ip link` command on the host undoes every VLAN you configured.

children.title: LAYER A - gVisor (the straitjacket)
lines: Application syscalls never reach the real host kernel - the Sentry emulates them in a Go userspace process (see the architecture diagram above)
What it does NOT catch: an attacker already inside the sandbox scanning the LOCAL network.

If this were the only layer: gVisor hands normal Ethernet frames to the host bridge - nothing stops the sandboxed app from nmap-scanning a neighboring tenant's container on the same unsegmented bridge.

children.title: Each layer's blind spot is exactly the next layer's job
lines: that's why all three run together, not any one alone.
